What is Heroin?

blocks.html: Heroin is classified as an opioid. For many, the use of heroin can be traced back to misuse and abuse of prescription painkillers, prescribed or not. Individuals who develop an addiction or physical dependency to opioids often begin to use heroin, as it is a cheaper alternative that can provide similar results to painkillers.

How Does Heroin Impact the Body?

blocks.html: The method used will impact the length of time it takes for the individual to begin experiencing the effects of heroin. As an example, using heroin intravenously will have faster results than smoking would.

blocks.html: No matter how heroin is used, the impact on the body will be the same. Heroin tells our brains to release a neurotransmitter called dopamine, which is known as the “feel-good” neurotransmitter. This can decrease the amount of physical pain a person experiences in addition to providing a euphoric effect that can make individuals feel calm and relaxed.

What Are the Signs of Heroin Addiction?

blocks.html:
If you suspect that a loved one may be struggling with heroin, you have likely picked up on a few warning signs. It is important to recognize that some of the symptoms associated with a heroin addiction could also be signs and symptoms of other mental health concerns. Because of this, it is important to be mindful of how you share your concerns with your loved one.

Some signs and symptoms associated with heroin abuse include:
- Restricted, or small, pupils
- Slurred speech
- Unexplained weight loss
- Unexplained bruising
- Increased irritability
- Inability to cut down, stop, or control use
- Withdrawing from family and friends
- Forgetting important events or dates
- New or worsening financial concerns
- Stealing
- Pawning belongings for cash
- New or worsening legal concerns

How Long Does It Take to Detox from Heroin?

blocks.html:
Individuals who have become physically dependent on heroin will begin to experience physical discomfort when they stop using. Detox centers are often recommended for individuals who have been abusing heroin to avoid experiencing medical complications, and to receive medication-assisted treatment that can help ease some of their symptoms.

Many individuals begin experiencing withdrawal symptoms within the first 24 hours of their last use. This will of course depend on the frequency and amount typically used. The first 1-2 days of the withdrawal period tend to be the most painful and have the highest risk for physical and mental health complications. This is a common time for individuals to relapse, due to the severe discomfort they may experience.

Within a week, opioids should fully be out of a person’s system. After the physical symptoms have become more tolerable, it is possible for mental health and physical health concerns to worsen.
